doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Playing with Shep Fields
summary: Auditioning as a hot player but hired for Fields's Rippling Rhythm band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Yes, absolutely. I took anything. I worked with Shep Fields. I got my three months in, in three months you’re not allowed to do anything, to get your card, three months on your transfer. The next three months you’re allowed to work with permission. And I had some friends from the Army who were working with Shep Fields’ band. I had never played that ricky-tick kind of, he called it “rippling rhythm.” And they were holding auditions. He was reorganizing his Rippling Rhythm band. They were holding auditions at Nola Studios in New York. So my friend said why don’t you come on up? So what would I audition for? The hot seat, right? The jazz player right? Which was nothing. He didn’t like me at all. But he said, “While you’re here,” he said, “why don’t you play the first book” you know. And that was the book that had [scats] and the Harmon mute and the bubbles going up and down and the accordion and everything. Perfect. So that’s what I did until I got my six months in. I worked it. And I didn’t dislike it in the sense that he knew what he wanted. I didn’t have to like what he wanted. He knew what he wanted and he knew how to get it.
Well there you go. What didn’t he like about your hot playing? Do you know? I mean was it maybe too modern for him?
Well I don’t know, I guess it wasn’t ricky-tick enough. So he X’d that right away.
He’ll put you in the middle seat. You’re already there.
